sections.heading: What this is
sections.body:
The editor owns the editorial calls; an automation operates the system. Each essay enters a tiered ladder of publications, tier 1 down to tier 3, and moves down on its own when a publication's window closes in silence. A piece no tier takes lands on the company journal plus an email send.
The whole ladder lives on one persistent checklist page that the editor can refer to at any time. Direction, set 2026-11-09: the checklist is the persistent home of the check-down, and the automation handles the sending and the progression. This page is the full design; the Decisions tab holds the questions that are still yours to answer.

sections.heading: 1 · The checklist — one source of truth
sections.body:
One persistent checklist page, "Essay check-down", in three sections:
- **The board** — one block per essay: title, byline (the columnist or the editor), link to the final text, current state, current publication and tier, editor name, sent date, window-end date, next action and its date, and a one-line history. This replaces the per-piece status log that never existed.
- **The publication book** — one block per publication: tier, editors and email, submission method (email vs web form), exclusivity terms, AI-authorship policy, normal response window, notes. Example already earned: one regional daily's essay desk is web-form only, and its tips@ address bounces.
- **Rules of the road** — the ratified ladder rules printed on the checklist itself, so the editor reads the same rules the automation executes.
The automation updates the checklist on every state change and posts the change in the team channel **with the checklist link** — the editor's standing ask. They never have to ask where a piece is.
Two hard constraints the board enforces:
- One live submission per piece (essay exclusivity).
- One live piece per publication at a time — never pitch a national daily a second columnist piece while one is already sitting there.

sections.heading: 2 · The two send paths — the missing functionality
sections.body:
Pitches and bulk sends are different kinds of email, and they need different pipes.
### A · Pitch path (one-to-one, to editors)
Sends **as the editor** — a pitch from an automation address kills credibility, and replies must thread back to the editor. Route: the workspace identity-email gateway (send as the editor's address). Status today: sending is **off**. The platform engineer's six gateway setup steps were never completed, and some of them need you or the ops lead. Until it lands, the automation drafts and posts an approval card and the editor sends. Once it lands, the automation sends directly under the approval model in section 4.
### B · Blast path (the fallback rung, and the newsletter)
Sends from the journal's mail domain via the bulk mail provider, on the Nov 5 design: a sending-only API key restricted to the journal domain, provisioned to the automation's VM through the existing team password vault item, plus a **send-email CLI** on the automation's VM that encodes the runbook — audience pull, 48-hour exclusion against the send log, suppression check, List-Unsubscribe header, batched send, send IDs returned so the automation can report opens and clicks itself. This same path carries the Nov 19 launch email, to about 2,140 subscribers.

sections.heading: 3 · How a piece moves — the state machine the automation runs
sections.body:
States per essay: **drafting → approved → live at tier N (window ends on a date) → placed, or next tier, or fallback → published on the journal + blast sent → done.**
- Window expiry means silence, and silence advances the piece to the next tier automatically. No withdrawal emails, ever — the editor's rule.
- Windows come from the publication book; the defaults come from the rules in section 5. News-pegged pieces move faster, 24 hours per top swing; a piece still unplaced by day 6 goes to the fallback.
- Before every send, the automation checks the publication's current AI-authorship policy and submission method in the publication book, and refreshes them if stale. Where AI text is barred, the automation briefs instead of drafting.
- Web-form publications cannot ride the email path. They become a manual task posted for the editor, with the form link and the exact text to paste.
- An editor's reply stops the clock. Replies land in the editor's inbox, which the automation cannot read — how they reach the automation is Round 1, question 4.
- Address hygiene: any bounce marks the publication-book entry bad, and the automation finds the current route before the next send. That rule exists because of one regional daily's bouncing tips@ address.

sections.heading: 4 · Approval model
sections.body:
- The editor approves each essay **once**: final text plus ladder order, recorded on the checklist. The columnist approves their own bylined text once — already the pattern. Claims in regulated topics keep the existing columnist gate.
- After that one approval, sends and advances are **notify-and-proceed**: the automation posts each send and each advance in the team channel with the checklist link. No per-send approval cards.
- The editor can pause or kill any essay with a word in its thread.
- Any edit to an approved text voids the approval and re-queues the piece for the editor.

sections.heading: 5 · Rules baked in — pending your ratification
sections.body:
Two rules from the pending candidate pile (automation-monitor) get baked into the automation. Ratifying them is Round 1, question 1.
- **Public first (2026-10-27):** consumer publications before trade, at the level the piece deserves; never let the clock lower the ladder. Move on only when the publication's own window ends or an editor releases it; never invent an "exclusive until" deadline.
- **Pitch-to-decay (2026-10-29):** two swings at the top, then the middle; news-pegged pieces get 24 hours per top swing, with the deadline stated politely; still unplaced by day 6, the piece runs on the company journal plus a professional-network post and email.
The Oct 27 candidate's self-set clock parts are superseded by the Oct 29 decay rule and drop out.

sections.heading: 6 · Deliberately out of v1
sections.body:
- **Rapid response / quote requests and the columnist quote bank** share the pitch send path once it exists, but they are a separate inbound lane. V2, on the same checklist as a second board if it earns it.
- **CMS-lite:** the fallback rung's journal publish still goes by PR until the CMS-lite pipe exists. The check-down does not wait for it.

sections.heading: 7 · Measurement
sections.body: The automation keeps a running tally on the checklist footer: sends, replies, and placements by publication and tier. Monthly, that data re-orders the tiers — publications that answer move up.

sections.heading: 8 · Build order
sections.body:
- **1. Checklist live** (automation, now): the board seeded with the 4 circulating pieces at their true current states; the publication book seeded from this week's sends.
- **2. Progression automation**: window timers, advance-on-silence, checklist upkeep, thread notifications.
- **3. Blast path** (send-email CLI plus scoped key): needed by Nov 19 regardless, for the launch email.
- **4. Pitch path** (identity gateway): unblocks fully automated pitching; the approval-card flow covers the gap until then.

questions.context: The two rules in section 5 of the design: public-first (consumer publications before trade, at the level the piece deserves, move on only at the publication's own window) and pitch-to-decay (two swings at the top, 24 hours per top swing for news-pegged pieces, unplaced by day 6 goes to journal + email). Ratifying bakes them into the automation.
